intro:
Each lesson follows the same pattern: (1) key vocabulary with meanings and examples, (2) useful phrases, (3) a model dialogue, (4) a gap-fill exercise, (5) discussion questions, (6) role-plays.

Suggested method: study the vocabulary, read the dialogue aloud twice, do Exercise A, then spend most of your time on Exercises B and C. Speaking is the goal.

Tip: record yourself, listen back, and repeat the exercise using at least eight new words from the lesson. Write your own example sentences about your real job.

Answers to Exercise A are at the end of the book. Discussion questions and role-plays have no single correct answer.

The two roadmaps are designed to be used together. Part A covers everyday workplace English in 4 modules. Part B develops a deeper 6-section programme (units 1-66). The unit numbers on the roadmap images were partly unclear, so the lessons follow the section themes.

lessons.title: Everyday Work & Workplaces
goals: Describe your job, duties and responsibilities clearly.
Talk about working hours, flexible schedules and remote work.
Describe different workplaces and types of workers.

vocabulary.meaning: the official name of your position
vocabulary.example: My job title is Marketing Assistant.

vocabulary.meaning: the tasks you must do in your job
vocabulary.example: One of my duties is answering customer emails.

vocabulary.meaning: having the job of looking after something
vocabulary.example: I'm responsible for the monthly budget.

vocabulary.meaning: managing or controlling a person or thing
vocabulary.example: She's in charge of a team of six.

vocabulary.meaning: to have someone as your direct manager
vocabulary.example: I report to the Sales Director.

vocabulary.meaning: a section of a company with a specific function
vocabulary.example: He works in the HR department.

vocabulary.meaning: a traditional, fixed working day
vocabulary.example: I don't want a nine-to-five job any more.

vocabulary.meaning: a system where you choose your start and finish times
vocabulary.example: With flexitime, I start at 7 and finish at 3.

vocabulary.meaning: work organised in fixed periods, e.g. day or night
vocabulary.example: Nurses often do shift work.

vocabulary.meaning: working from home using the internet and phone
vocabulary.example: Telecommuting saves me two hours a day.

vocabulary.meaning: extra hours worked beyond normal hours
vocabulary.example: We worked a lot of overtime before the launch.

vocabulary.meaning: a large office space with no walls between desks
vocabulary.example: Open-plan offices can be noisy.

vocabulary.meaning: someone who does office or professional work
vocabulary.example: Accountants are white-collar workers.

vocabulary.meaning: someone whose job involves physical work
vocabulary.example: Manual workers need good safety equipment.

vocabulary.meaning: to travel regularly between home and work
vocabulary.example: I commute by train for 40 minutes.

vocabulary.meaning: the date or time by which work must be finished
vocabulary.example: The deadline for the report is Friday.

phrases: I work as a... / I'm a... in the ... department.
My main responsibilities include...
I'm in charge of... / I'm responsible for...
I usually start at... and finish at...
I work from home two days a week.
Could you tell me who's in charge of...?
Who do you report to?
I'm on the late shift this week.

dialogue.speaker: Anna
dialogue.line: So, what do you do, Marco?

dialogue.speaker: Marco
dialogue.line: I'm a project coordinator. I'm in charge of schedules and I report to the Operations Manager.

dialogue.speaker: Anna
dialogue.line: Do you work nine-to-five?

dialogue.speaker: Marco
dialogue.line: Not exactly. We have flexitime, so I start at 8 and finish at 4. And I telecommute on Fridays.

dialogue.speaker: Anna
dialogue.line: That sounds great. I work in an open-plan office and it's very noisy!

dialogue.speaker: Marco
dialogue.line: Well, the commute is the real problem for me. It takes an hour each way.

lessons.exerciseALead: Word bank: duty | flexitime | in charge of | manual | shift | telecommuting
exerciseA: 1. My manager is __________ the whole sales team; she decides who works on which project.
2. I do not have fixed hours. My company offers __________, so I can choose when to start.
3. Doctors and factory staff often do __________ work, including nights.
4. It is my __________ to prepare the weekly report.
5. During the pandemic, many teachers started __________ for the first time.
6. Lorenzo is a __________ worker; he repairs machines in the factory.
lessons.exerciseBLead: Discuss in pairs or small groups, or record your answers aloud (1-2 minutes each). Give reasons and examples.
exerciseB: 1. Describe your job (or the job you want). What are your main duties and who do you report to?
2. Do you prefer a nine-to-five routine or flexitime? Explain your reasons.
3. What are the advantages and disadvantages of telecommuting for employees and for companies?
4. Would you prefer to work in an open-plan office or a private office? Why?
5. Is a white-collar job always better than a manual job? Discuss.
6. How long is your commute? What could make it better?
7. How do you cope with tight deadlines? Give an example.
exerciseC: Role-play A: You meet a new colleague at a company event. Introduce your job, your department, your responsibilities and your usual working hours. Ask about theirs.
Role-play B: Your manager proposes changing the team from a nine-to-five schedule to flexitime. One person supports the idea; the other has concerns. Discuss and agree on rules.
lessons.answers: 1. in charge of; 2. flexitime; 3. shift; 4. duty; 5. telecommuting; 6. manual

lessons.title: The Talent Pipeline
goals: Talk about recruitment, hiring and the application process.
Describe your personal qualities and professional skills.
Discuss career progression, promotion and restructuring.

I'd like to apply for the vacancy advertised on...
I have X years of experience in...
One of my strengths is...; one area I'm improving is...
I'm a quick learner and a team player.
Where do you see yourself in five years?
Could you tell me more about the opportunities for promotion?
We'd like to offer you the position.

dialogue.line: Thank you for coming. Tell me about your background.

dialogue.speaker: Candidate
dialogue.line: I have five years' experience in customer service. I'm proactive and I enjoy working in a team.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.line: Why are you leaving your current job?

dialogue.speaker: Candidate
dialogue.line: After the restructuring, there are few opportunities for promotion, and I want to move up the career ladder.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer

dialogue.speaker: Candidate

lessons.exerciseALead: Word bank: applicants | CV | probation | restructuring | self-motivated | vacancy
exerciseA: 1. The company posted a __________ for a sales manager on its website.
2. A __________ usually lists your education, skills and work experience.
3. We shortlisted six candidates from the 150 __________.
4. Maria does not need supervision. She is very __________.
5. After the __________, many managers lost their jobs.
6. New employees often have a three-month __________ period.
lessons.exerciseBLead: Discuss in pairs or small groups, or record your answers aloud (1-2 minutes each). Give reasons and examples.
exerciseB: 1. Describe the best job advertisement you have seen. What made it attractive?

lessons.title: Compensation & Workplace Challenges

Raise and discuss workplace problems politely.

vocabulary.meaning: payment calculated per hour or week

vocabulary.meaning: pay before / after tax and deductions

vocabulary.meaning: extra money paid for good performance

vocabulary.meaning: the right to buy company shares at a fixed price

vocabulary.meaning: regular payments after you retire

vocabulary.meaning: an increase in salary

vocabulary.meaning: rules to protect people at work

vocabulary.meaning: something that can cause harm

vocabulary.meaning: being treated with respect at work

vocabulary.meaning: unwanted behaviour that offends or intimidates

vocabulary.meaning: unfair treatment based on gender, age, race, etc.
vocabulary.example: Age discrimination is illegal.

vocabulary.meaning: the same chances for everyone

vocabulary.meaning: a healthy balance between work and personal life

vocabulary.meaning: extreme exhaustion caused by overwork

vocabulary.meaning: a formal complaint made by an employee
vocabulary.example: She filed a grievance against her manager.

phrases: I'd like to discuss my salary / a possible pay rise.
Based on my results this year, I believe I deserve...
The package includes health insurance and 25 days' holiday.
I'd like to report a safety concern.
I don't feel this is fair / in line with our policy.
Everyone should have equal opportunities.
I'm finding the workload difficult to manage.
Could we find a solution together?

dialogue.speaker: Employee
dialogue.line: Do you have a few minutes? I'd like to talk about my pay.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.line: Of course. What did you want to discuss?

dialogue.speaker: Employee
dialogue.line: I've exceeded my targets, and I now manage two juniors. I'd like to request a pay rise.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.line: You've done excellent work. I can't change your salary now, but I can offer extra benefits.

dialogue.speaker: Employee
dialogue.line: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.line: Stock options and one extra week of holiday. Would that interest you?

lessons.exerciseALead: Word bank: commission | discrimination | fringe | hazard | salary | wage
exerciseA: 1. Her __________ is 3,000 euros a month, paid on the 28th.
2. Factory staff are often paid an hourly __________.
3. In addition to pay, we offer __________ benefits such as private health insurance.
4. Sales staff earn a 5% __________ on every contract.
5. A loose cable on the floor is a safety __________.
6. Treating colleagues differently because of their age is __________.
lessons.exerciseBLead: Discuss in pairs or small groups, or record your answers aloud (1-2 minutes each). Give reasons and examples.
exerciseB: 1. Salary or fringe benefits: which matters more to you? Why?
2. What is a fair salary for your job? How would you ask for a pay rise?
3. Are stock options a good way to motivate employees? What are the risks?
4. What are the main health and safety risks in your workplace or in an office?
5. How can companies promote equal opportunities and prevent discrimination?
6. What does 'dignity at work' mean to you? Give examples of respectful and disrespectful behaviour.
7. How can employees avoid burnout and keep a good work-life balance?
exerciseC: Role-play A: Salary negotiation. The employee asks for a pay rise and explains why; the manager responds with limits and an alternative benefit.
Role-play B: An employee reports a safety hazard. The manager asks questions, takes the concern seriously and decides on an action plan.
lessons.answers: 1. salary; 2. wage; 3. fringe; 4. commission; 5. hazard; 6. discrimination

lessons.title: Leadership & Corporate Structures

The company is owned by... / is a subsidiary of...

I'd like to delegate this task to you.

dialogue.speaker: Journalist
dialogue.line: How did your company start?

dialogue.speaker: Founder
dialogue.line: I started as a sole trader, selling coffee online. Two years later I formed an LLC with a partner.

dialogue.speaker: Journalist
dialogue.line: And now?

dialogue.speaker: Founder
dialogue.line: We're an SME with 80 employees, and we've just opened a subsidiary in Canada.

dialogue.speaker: Journalist

lessons.exerciseALead: Word bank: CEO | charity | delegate | headquarters | SMEs | sole trader
exerciseA: 1. The __________ reports to the board of directors and runs the company day to day.
2. A __________ owns and runs the business alone and is personally responsible for debts.
3. The company's __________ is in London, but it has offices worldwide.
4. A good manager must know how to __________ tasks to the team.
5. Most local firms are __________ with fewer than 250 employees.

lessons.exerciseBLead: Discuss in pairs or small groups, or record your answers aloud (1-2 minutes each). Give reasons and examples.

3. What are the advantages and risks of being a sole trader versus an LLC?

dialogue.speaker: Sara

dialogue.line: Congratulations! What's the management style like?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Very democratic. My manager always asks for our ideas before making a decision.

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.line: That's rare. My boss is autocratic; he decides everything alone.

dialogue.speaker: Tom

vocabulary.meaning: gross domestic product: total value of a country's output

vocabulary.meaning: a general rise in prices

vocabulary.meaning: the cost of borrowing money

vocabulary.meaning: a period of economic decline

vocabulary.meaning: the value of one currency against another

We're showing a healthy profit / a loss of...
Our assets exceed our liabilities.

dialogue.speaker: Analyst
dialogue.line: What were your results this year?

dialogue.speaker: CFO
dialogue.line: Revenue grew by 12%, and our profit margin improved to 9%.

dialogue.speaker: Analyst
dialogue.line: And the balance sheet?

dialogue.speaker: CFO
dialogue.line: Assets increased and liabilities fell. Cash flow is strong, so we'll pay a higher dividend.

dialogue.speaker: Analyst
dialogue.line: What about the acquisition you announced?

dialogue.speaker: CFO
dialogue.line: It should be completed next quarter, subject to shareholder approval.

lessons.exerciseALead: Word bank: acquisition | assets | balance | dividend | inflation | loss
exerciseA: 1. If costs are higher than income, the company makes a __________.
2. A __________ sheet shows what a company owns and what it owes.

5. A rise in prices over time is called __________.
6. Shareholders receive a __________ from company profits.
lessons.exerciseBLead: Discuss in pairs or small groups, or record your answers aloud (1-2 minutes each). Give reasons and examples.
exerciseB: 1. What is the difference between revenue and profit? Why can a company have high revenue and still lose money?
2. Why is cash flow so important for small businesses?
3. Why do companies merge or acquire others? What can go wrong?

5. How does inflation affect ordinary people and businesses?

exerciseC: Role-play A: Present your company's annual results to shareholders. Use trend language (rose, fell, remained stable) and answer questions.

lessons.answers: 1. loss; 2. balance; 3. assets; 4. acquisition; 5. inflation; 6. dividend

lessons.title: Professional Integrity & Self-Management
goals: Discuss ethics, corporate responsibility and corruption.
Talk about stress, time management and well-being.
Describe leadership styles and personal skills.

vocabulary.meaning: moral principles about right and wrong
vocabulary.example: The company has a strict code of ethics.

vocabulary.meaning: a company's duty to society and the environment
vocabulary.example: CSR is part of our brand.

vocabulary.meaning: meeting needs without harming the future
vocabulary.example: Sustainability guides our supply choices.

vocabulary.meaning: dishonest behaviour by people with power
vocabulary.example: The minister was accused of corruption.

vocabulary.meaning: money given illegally to get an advantage
vocabulary.example: He refused to take a bribe.

vocabulary.meaning: deception to make illegal gain
vocabulary.example: The accountant committed fraud.

vocabulary.meaning: an employee who reports wrongdoing
vocabulary.example: The whistleblower exposed illegal waste dumping.

vocabulary.meaning: a situation where personal gain affects judgement
vocabulary.example: Owning shares in a supplier is a conflict of interest.

vocabulary.meaning: openness about how decisions are made
vocabulary.example: Transparency builds trust.

vocabulary.meaning: mental pressure caused by demands
vocabulary.example: Heavy workloads cause stress.

vocabulary.meaning: to decide what is most important
vocabulary.example: Prioritise your tasks each morning.

vocabulary.meaning: using your time effectively
vocabulary.example: Good time management reduces pressure.

vocabulary.meaning: to do several things at once
vocabulary.example: I can't multitask during meetings.

vocabulary.meaning: to become exhausted by overwork
vocabulary.example: Don't burn yourself out.

vocabulary.meaning: being comfortable, healthy and happy
vocabulary.example: The company offers well-being programmes.

vocabulary.meaning: to work efficiently, not just longer
vocabulary.example: Learn to work smarter, not harder.

phrases: It's against company policy to...
We have a zero-tolerance policy on bribery.
I think we should disclose this conflict of interest.
I'm under a lot of pressure at the moment.
Let me prioritise my tasks.
I have too much on my plate.
Could we move the deadline?
I'm trying to keep a healthy work-life balance.

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.line: I found something strange in the accounts. A supplier received double payments.

dialogue.speaker: Nina
dialogue.line: That could be fraud. Have you told Compliance?

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.line: Not yet. I'm afraid of causing trouble.

dialogue.speaker: Nina
dialogue.line: Our policy protects whistleblowers. It's the ethical thing to do.

dialogue.speaker: Ravi
dialogue.line: You're right. I'll report it today.

dialogue.speaker: Nina
dialogue.line: Good. And take a break afterwards; you look stressed.

lessons.exerciseALead: Word bank: bribe | conflict | CSR | prioritise | transparency | whistleblower
exerciseA: 1. Giving money to an official for a favour is a __________.

4. To manage my workload, I __________ the most urgent tasks first.
5. Taking responsibility toward society and the environment is called __________.
6. Being open about decisions and finances is called __________.
lessons.exerciseBLead: Discuss in pairs or small groups, or record your answers aloud (1-2 minutes each). Give reasons and examples.
exerciseB: 1. Why do companies need a code of ethics? What should it include?
2. Have you ever faced an ethical dilemma at work or school? What did you do?
3. Should whistleblowers be protected by law? Why?
4. How can companies reduce their environmental impact?
5. What are the main causes of stress at work? How can you reduce it?
6. What are your best time management techniques?
7. Which leadership style do you prefer to work under?
exerciseC: Role-play A: A supplier offers you an expensive gift before a contract decision. Refuse politely and explain company policy.
Role-play B: A colleague looks exhausted and overloaded. Offer support, suggest ways to prioritise, and propose speaking to the manager.
lessons.answers: 1. bribe; 2. whistleblower; 3. conflict; 4. prioritise; 5. CSR; 6. transparency

lessons.title: The Global Communicator: Culture & Tools
goals: Navigate etiquette and cultural differences in business.
Use the telephone professionally.
Write clear, polite business emails and arrange meetings.

vocabulary.meaning: accepted rules of polite behaviour
vocabulary.example: Business etiquette differs between countries.

vocabulary.meaning: rules about what to wear
vocabulary.example: The dress code is smart casual.

vocabulary.meaning: arriving on time
vocabulary.example: Be punctual; Germans value it.

vocabulary.meaning: polite, informal conversation
vocabulary.example: We made small talk before the meeting.

vocabulary.meaning: welcoming guests, e.g. meals and entertainment
vocabulary.example: The hospitality was excellent.

vocabulary.meaning: a card with your name and contact details
vocabulary.example: He handed me his business card.

vocabulary.meaning: serious and polite / relaxed in style
vocabulary.example: Use a formal tone with new clients.

vocabulary.meaning: wait on the telephone
vocabulary.example: Could you hold the line, please?

vocabulary.meaning: connect a caller to someone
vocabulary.example: I'll put you through to Sales.

vocabulary.meaning: ask someone to pass on information
vocabulary.example: Can I leave a message?

vocabulary.meaning: a recorded phone message system
vocabulary.example: I got your voicemail.

vocabulary.meaning: the title of an email

vocabulary.meaning: a file sent with an email

vocabulary.meaning: copy / blind copy of an email

vocabulary.meaning: answer every recipient of an email

vocabulary.meaning: to make certain / to change a date

vocabulary.meaning: a plan for an event or meeting

lessons.title: Advanced Mastery: High-Level Business Skills
goals: Lead and take part in effective meetings.
Prepare and deliver a clear presentation, including Q
A.
Negotiate and reach a final agreement.

vocabulary.meaning: a list of topics to discuss in a meeting
vocabulary.example: Let's follow the agenda.

vocabulary.meaning: to lead a meeting; the person who does so
vocabulary.example: Who's chairing the meeting?

vocabulary.meaning: an official record of a meeting
vocabulary.example: Please send the minutes.

vocabulary.meaning: tasks agreed during a meeting
vocabulary.example: The action points are listed below.

vocabulary.meaning: the last agenda item for extra topics
vocabulary.example: Under AOB, I'd like to raise one point.

vocabulary.meaning: to agree as a group
vocabulary.example: We reached a consensus on the budget.

vocabulary.meaning: phrases that guide the audience through a talk
vocabulary.example: Good signposting helps listeners follow.

vocabulary.meaning: a single page of a presentation
vocabulary.example: On this slide, you can see the results.

vocabulary.meaning: time for questions and answers
vocabulary.example: We'll have a short Q & A at the end.

vocabulary.meaning: a chart or image used to support a talk
vocabulary.example: Use visual aids to clarify data.

vocabulary.meaning: a formal suggestion or offer
vocabulary.example: We've submitted a proposal.

vocabulary.meaning: something you give up in a negotiation
vocabulary.example: We made a concession on delivery time.

vocabulary.meaning: a new offer in response to another
vocabulary.example: They made a counteroffer of 90,000.

vocabulary.meaning: something used to gain an advantage
vocabulary.example: Early payment is our bargaining chip.

vocabulary.meaning: a condition that ends negotiations if not met
vocabulary.example: Exclusivity is a deal-breaker.

vocabulary.meaning: an agreement where each side gives something up
vocabulary.example: Let's find a compromise.

vocabulary.meaning: a result good for both sides
vocabulary.example: We want a win-win solution.

vocabulary.meaning: the details of an agreement
vocabulary.example: Please check the terms and conditions.

phrases: Let's get started. The first item on the agenda is...
Could I come in here? / Let me finish my point.
I see your point, but I'm afraid I disagree because...
Today I'm going to talk about... First,... Then,... Finally,...
Let's move on to the next slide / Turning to...
That's a good question. Let me explain...
We could offer... if you could agree to...
Let's summarise what we've agreed.

dialogue.speaker: Buyer
dialogue.line: Your price is too high. We were thinking of 80,000.

dialogue.speaker: Seller
dialogue.line: I understand, but quality is our priority. We could do 90,000 with free delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Buyer
dialogue.line: That's closer. If we sign a two-year contract, could you go down to 85,000?

dialogue.speaker: Seller
dialogue.line: A longer contract is attractive. I could agree to 87,000 with payment in 30 days.

dialogue.speaker: Buyer
dialogue.line: I think we can live with that.

dialogue.speaker: Seller
dialogue.line: Excellent. Let's summarise the terms and I'll send the contract today.

lessons.exerciseBLead: Discuss in pairs or small groups, or record your answers aloud (1-2 minutes each). Give reasons and examples.
